newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine property firm C&P Homes widens focus.
newsitem.headline: Philippine property firm C&P Homes widens focus.

text.p: Philippine developer C&P Homes Inc aims to sharply increase its share of the country's buoyant market for middle-income housing, chief financial officer John Huang told Reuters on Friday.
Middle-income housing accounted for 18 to 20 percent of C&P sales in 1995 and 4.0 percent in 1994. "This year, it will probably account for 30 percent," Huang said.

C&P, which normally specialises in low-cost housing, defines middle-income properties as those that cost about 1.0 million pesos. This compares with Philippine real estate giant Ayala Land's definition of 1.5 to 5.0 million pesos.
Huang said the market had interpreted the company's move as a "massive shift in strategy", but stressed: "We're still predominantly a low-cost housing developer.
"This segment of middle-income housing is a natural extension of our low-cost focus."
He said demand for middle-range housing in the Philippines had been spurred by higher incomes and the fact that banks were more willing to finance property purchases.
Due to the higher proportion of middle-income housing, Huang said the company had revised its forecast for unit sales this year to 25,000 from 27,000.
"The sales mix has improved," he said, adding that this did not mean a change in earnings targets for 1996.
"We think we will earn 2.7 billion pesos on revenues of 9.0 billion pesos. We're on track to meeting these targets," he said. In 1995, the company made a net income of 2.011 billion pesos.
He expected net profit for the first nine months of the year to be close to 2.0 billion pesos on unit sales of 17,000.
C&P posted a net income of 1.421 billion pesos from revenues of 4.968 billion pesos in the nine-month period last year.
The company aims to sell 30,000 housing units next year.
Net income could rise by 15 percent to 3.1 billion pesos next year, while revenues could increase by 22 percent to 11 billion pesos, Huang said.
C&P Homes had about 3,100 hectares in its land bank, "enough land for the next five to eight years," Huang said.
